analysis.one_liner: Bars accounting firms from selling consulting services to companies they audit.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or a vote, and it never drew a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Securities and Exchange Commission to stop treating an accounting firm as an independent auditor if that firm also sells consulting or other non-audit services to the company it audits. The concern it addressed is that an auditor paid millions for consulting work has a financial stake in keeping the client happy, which can color its judgment about the client's financial statements. The bill was introduced after Enron's collapse, was sent to a House subcommittee in March 2002, and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors, including people with pensions and 401(k)s tied to public company stock, would benefit from more honest audits. If an auditor cannot also earn consulting fees from its audit client, it has less financial reason to overlook accounting problems in the client's books.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the SEC to stop treating an accounting firm as independent if it performs non-audit services for the company whose financial statements it certifies.
Requires the SEC to define 'non-audit services' and issue implementing rules within 90 days of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Large accounting firms would bear the cost, giving up lucrative consulting and other non-audit fees from the same companies they audit. Public companies would pay more to buy advisory services from separate firms rather than bundling them with their auditor.

drawbacks.text: The bill bans all non-audit services outright and leaves the SEC to define that term, which could sweep in benign services like routine tax preparation that do not threaten auditor independence; the approach Congress later enacted banned a specific list of services instead of all of them.

A blanket prohibition could raise costs for smaller public companies with fewer accounting firms to choose from, since their auditor and their tax or advisory work would have to come from different firms.
By leaving the entire definition to SEC rulemaking on a 90-day clock, the bill deferred the hard policy choices to regulators rather than making them in statute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is sound: an auditor that earns consulting fees from its audit client has a financial interest in keeping that client happy, and the Enron collapse showed how dangerous that can be for people whose savings ride on honest audits. But the bill was a blunt instrument — a total ban on all non-audit services, with the definition left to the SEC — and it was introduced without any cosponsors and never taken up. Its substance resurfaced later in 2002 in the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, which took the narrower approach of banning a specific list of non-audit services.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to a House Financial Services subcommittee in March 2002 and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sheila Jackson-Lee introduced the bill on February 7, 2002, weeks after the Enron collapse focused national attention on auditor independence.
The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced.
On March 4, 2002, it was referred to the Capital Markets, Insurance and Government Sponsored Enterprises Subcommittee, where it stayed.
The bill attracted no cosponsors and no committee action for the rest of the 107th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large accounting firms were better off, since they kept collecting consulting fees from the companies they audited throughout 2002. Investors did not get the ban from this bill; a version of the same restriction was enacted months later in the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, which banned specific non-audit services rather than all of them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Accounting firms kept consulting revenue from audit clients

for.name: Sheila Jackson-Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its only sponsor; it was referred to committee the same day.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over securities regulation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Capital Markets, Insurance and Government Sponsored Enterprises Subcommittee on March 4, 2002, where it remained without a hearing or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no party split is recorded; a Democratic member introduced it alone and no Republican or Democrat signed on.

industries.note: Audit firms earned large sums selling consulting and other non-audit services to their own audit clients, an arrangement the Enron scandal showed could compromise audits. The bill would cut off that revenue stream by directing the SEC to strip auditor status from firms providing such services.

The bill restricts which services a public company can bundle with its audit, which would raise compliance friction and force companies to buy advisory work from separate providers. A cleaner audit serves the companies' own investors, so the effect on issuers cuts both ways.
